text: GoLive proves that a system exists, but it doesn't prove the people behind the work will actually use it or that it will ever deliver a single dollar from the deal model.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I am Michelle Grant, creator of Leading at Scale.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the question every enterprise is confronting right now is the age it works.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Does anyone trust it?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I have spent over 20 years in enterprise transformation and more than a decade leading M&A integrations across media, tech, and consumer goods.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: On those deals, trust was not something we crossed our fingers and hoped for after launch.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We engineered it before day one through early change management and risk management.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So when the platform went live, the teams on the ground actually relied on it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: AI agents demand the exact same muscle.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: An agent earns trust when it delivers the value the business budgeted for while staying strictly within the company's approved risk appetite, policies, and regulatory guardrails.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In my experience, leadership gets there by answering three straightforward questions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What value does it create?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Who is on the hook for it?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what evidence gives it permission to run with greater autonomy?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The moment an agent steps out of a sandbox and into a core business workflow, the entire test changes.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A pilot tests whether the software functions, but daily operations is where we test whether it creates value within the controls set by leadership.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Established AI risk frameworks give you strong principles.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What they do not give you is how to apply these principles to each agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For every agent, leadership has to decide four things.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What is it permitted to do?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Who owns it?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What evidence it records?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what triggers an escalation?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That work is not an engineering task.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We find it is an executive operating mandate.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And today I'll show you how to meet it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Let us ground this in a real world scenario.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Picture a $15 billion acquisition targeting 400 million in net synergies.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The deal has already closed and the integration efforts are now underway.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The Integration Management Office, which we'll also refer to as the IMO today, is driving the synergy roadmap across 40 work streams.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Covering everything from rationalizing vendor contracts to consolidating ERP systems.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And every single initiative has a business owner accountable for its bottom line savings.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every week, analysts in the IMO are going to reconcile the numbers against the general ledger as they track down status from all 40 leads.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: They're also comparing actuals against the plan, then finally assembling the executive deck for the steering committee.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Which is going to include the CFO, the chief risk officer, business unit heads, and the integration lead.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The engineering team builds an agent to automate that first draft.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The agent then ingests the weekly updates, reconciles the ledger, runs variance map against the plan, and flags the initiatives that are falling behind.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Everything looks good and they decide to run a four-week pilot.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The agent's drafts match the analyst's reports, line for line.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So we can say that the tech works.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Now, the question is, what value does that steering committee need before they can trust it to run the business?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First, the steering committee needs a written value case.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Agreed upon before the agent ever touches production data.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In our example, that comes down to three specific metrics.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First, let's look at cycle time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If that weekly report eats five business days to compile right now, you're going to want to set a hard target such as two days.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your second metric will be analyst capacity.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If four analysts spend half of their week building the stack, that is 80 hours a week the agent gives back.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That time counts as value only when the integration lead assigns it to the work streams that are behind on their synergy targets and need help getting back on track.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then you only count that value after netting out the compute, licensing, and human review costs of running the agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your third metric is the most important one, detection time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: That is how long it takes from the first sign of a slip in the data to the moment the steering committee sees it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Cutting the report from five days to two days does not guarantee that the committee sees that slip any sooner.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The agent has to catch it, and the value case measures that directly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Every single metric requires a pre-deployment baseline.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If the IMO cannot state the baseline today, do not deploy.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If you can't measure where you started, you can never prove the agent moved the needle.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Next, the steering committee needs to know who owns the risk the agent creates.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: We are going to apply the three-line model to the agent.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In the first line, management owns the controls.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The integration lead is the accountable executive.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: She owns the agent's output exactly the way she owned the manual deck.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In the second line, risk and compliance oversee the agent and challenge how to run it.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: How deep they go depends on the agent's exposure.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: An internal draft scrubbed by a senior analyst warrants a very different review standard than an autonomous agent publishing figures straight to the board.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In the third line, internal audit provides assurance deciding based on material risk when and how the agent enters the annual audit plan.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The agent also needs one employee assigned to oversee it every day.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In our example, that is the senior analyst.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: He reviews the draft before it reaches the community.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Her role requires four specific capabilities.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: She has to first understand the operational boundaries.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: She has to interpret its output with context.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: She must have the authority to override or reverse it, and she needs a clear kill switch to shut it down safely the second it behaves unexpectedly.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Accountability also means defining where the agent's authority stops.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I document this in a one-page policy called the Human Works Standard.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For every fork in the process, it maps the decision the human role authorized to make it, the required evidence, and the escalation path.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: These decisions exist at every tier.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The senior analyst decides whether a variance is an accounting timing difference or a real cash shortfall.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The work stream lead decides how to remediate that shortfall.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And the integration lead is going to decide whether to formally flag an initiative as at risk to the steering committee.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The agent prepares the analysis behind every one of those decisions and it stops there.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The person who makes the decision owns the consequence.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So keeping these decisions with your team does not slow the agent down.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It can go into use while each role keeps its authority.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The one reason to delay deployments is a decision with no assigned owner.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This means if leadership has not agreed who declares an initiative off track, the agent's flags lead to no action.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The third question is where the engineers in this room come in.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The evidence for greater autonomy comes from how the agent is built.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: I look for three artifacts.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The first is an auditable decision log.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: For every work stream the agent evaluates, it records the raw data ingested.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The tool crawls executed, the prompt and the model versions, output generated along with the human sign-off.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Two engineering choices make that log airtight.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: First, your core math and reconciliation rules must run in deterministic finance-approved code, not generated as conversational prose from an LLM.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Second, treat the model's written summary as a helpful explanation, not proof.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your real proof lives in the telemetry.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What records were pulled?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What deterministic tools ran?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And who signed the review?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: If reported savings do not match the general ledger, agent does not touch the number.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It flats discrepancy and roots it up.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The second artifact is the model inventory record.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: This captures the accountable executive, data lineage, dependencies across source systems, validation results, escalation path, and the kill switch runbook.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Most importantly, it documents your regression triggers, which are any updates to our prompt, base model, or source API that require full revalidation before running in production again.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Your third artifact, this is going to be the autonomy scorecard.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The steering committee uses it to grant autonomy in four stages.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Stage one is shadow mode.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The analysts build the report as they do today.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The agent runs right alongside them and the team compares the two.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Stage two is the supervised draft.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The agent compiles the first draft and the senior analyst reviews every single line item.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Stage three is the exception and sample where the analyst reviews flagged initiatives plus a random sample of the claims.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Then we have stage four where it's exceptions only.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The analyst reviews only high risk anomalies supported by periodic independent sampling.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Pay close attention to stage four, however, because once humans only look at exceptions, your biggest vulnerability is what the agent failed to flag.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So I advise tracking missed material issues through independent sampling, monitoring error severity, and watching your override rate carefully.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: A falling override rate does not automatically mean the agent is getting smarter.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: It can also mean the depth of review has split.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So independent sampling tells you which one of these you are seeing.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: The scorecard puts those control metrics side by side with your value metrics, cycle time, analyst hours deployed, and your detection time.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And with that single page view, the steering committee can make clean, efficient data-backed decisions to either promote the agent, hold it where it is, step it back, or down to supervised review stage.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: So let's come back to the three questions.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Ask them of every agent you build, fund or govern.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: What value does it create?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Who is accountable for it?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: And what evidence permits it to operate with autonomy?
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: In our M&A example today, the agent does not magically create the 400 million in synergies.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Procurement, supply chain, and operating leaders capture that value through the gritty work of integration.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: But what the agent delivers is clear.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Verified evidence weeks ahead of schedule, giving leadership the runway to intervene while the deal's synergies can still be captured.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Building an agent that works is just the first step.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Answering those three questions is what earns it the trust to run at scale.
speaker: SPEAKER_00

text: Thank you.
